episodes.source_idea_paraphrase: Godin emphasizes the narrative surrounding available choices. His broad claim about helplessness being a story is a perspective, not an established universal psychological fact.

psychology_source.title: A Reward-Based Framework of Perceived Control - PubMed

episodes.narration_kind: Original educational adaptation; not a quotation or imitation of the author

scenes.narration: You send another application. No answer. Soon, every opportunity looks closed.
scenes.visual: An original avatar watches unanswered messages stack into a wall.

scenes.narration: Seth Godin asks us to examine the story around our choices.
scenes.visual: The wall opens into a board of options; no depiction of Godin.

scenes.narration: Perceived control means how much influence we believe we have over what happens.
scenes.visual: Overlay the term after rendering; distinguish expectation from outcome.

scenes.narration: You cannot make an employer reply. You might improve one application or ask for feedback.
scenes.visual: Employer response stays outside a small circle; preparation and support appear inside.

scenes.narration: A new action may reveal an option. It does not erase unfair systems or guarantee a job.
scenes.visual: One route becomes visible; barriers remain in frame.

scenes.narration: Ask: what can I influence today, and what help would make that action possible?
scenes.visual: Avatar connects with a mentor; hold reflection and source end card.

psychology_source.title: Throwing good effort after bad: Evidence for a sunk-cost effect in cognitive effort-based decision-making - PubMed

episodes.narration_kind: Original educational adaptation; not a quotation or imitation of the author

scenes.narration: You spent months on a project. Leaving now feels like throwing those months away.
scenes.visual: Avatar carries a backpack of calendar pages toward a fork.

scenes.narration: Seth Godin suggests judging the next investment from where you are now.
scenes.visual: Future path lights up; previous calendar pages remain behind.

scenes.narration: The sunk-cost effect is letting unrecoverable past costs weigh too heavily on a new decision.
scenes.visual: Label past cost and future value separately.

scenes.narration: Ask what the next month could accomplish here, compared with another realistic option.
scenes.visual: Two future plans appear side by side; camera follows the comparison.

scenes.narration: Past effort can teach you. It cannot, by itself, make the next step worthwhile.
scenes.visual: Avatar keeps a notebook of lessons and sets down the heavy backpack.

scenes.narration: What would you choose today if your past investment were already accounted for?
scenes.visual: Hold the fork, reflection, and source card; neither route is automatically declared correct.

scenes.narration: The plan failed. One person says everything is ruined. Another says everything is fine.
scenes.visual: Two speech bubbles compete over a broken bridge.

scenes.narration: Seth Godin offers a more useful question: where can we contribute and improve?
scenes.visual: Avatar examines the bridge rather than repeating either bubble.

scenes.narration: Optimism involves favorable expectations. It is different from pretending obstacles have disappeared.
scenes.visual: Show the technical term beside the visibly damaged bridge.

scenes.narration: A team checks the damage, gathers tools, and tests one possible repair.
scenes.visual: Three original avatars work together; progress is tentative.

scenes.narration: Confidence alone cannot rebuild a bridge. Plans, resources, and feedback still matter.
scenes.visual: Camera reveals materials, inspection checklist and remaining gap.

scenes.narration: What useful action fits the facts you have, while leaving room for a better outcome?
scenes.visual: One repaired section supports a test; hold reflection and source credits.

scenes.narration: You have an idea, but imagining the criticism stops you before you begin.
scenes.visual: Avatar holds a draft; imagined comment bubbles crowd the doorway.

scenes.narration: Seth Godin names fear as one obstacle that can keep useful work from happening.
scenes.visual: Bubbles shrink enough to reveal a possible first step.

scenes.narration: Fear responds to perceived danger. Sometimes that danger is judgment rather than physical harm.
scenes.visual: Label fear; imagined audience stays distinct from the actual room.

scenes.narration: A small rehearsal with someone you trust can make the next step more concrete.
scenes.visual: Avatar practices with a supportive friend; no guarantee of confidence.

scenes.narration: Some risks need protection or a different plan. Courage includes assessing the situation.
scenes.visual: Show a risk checklist and an alternate route.

scenes.narration: What are you afraid will happen, and what would make a first attempt reasonable?
scenes.visual: Avatar chooses whether to rehearse; reflection and sources finish the scene.

scenes.narration: You want life to feel different, but different has no shape yet.
scenes.visual: Avatar faces a foggy signpost with many unnamed paths.

scenes.narration: Napoleon Hill placed a definite purpose at the center of his approach.
scenes.visual: A single chosen destination appears; no reenactment of Hill.

scenes.narration: Purpose is a sense of direction toward something meaningful. A goal makes one part concrete.
scenes.visual: Overlay purpose and a specific goal as distinct labels.

scenes.narration: Instead of get better at everything, choose: complete one course module this week.
scenes.visual: Calendar shows one feasible study block and a module checkpoint.

scenes.narration: Writing the aim does not guarantee the result. Time, skill and support shape what is possible.
scenes.visual: Show the calendar beside resources and available help.

scenes.narration: What matters to you, and what would count as one realistic step toward it?
scenes.visual: Fog clears around the next step only; hold reflection and source card.

episodes.narration_kind: Original educational adaptation; not a quotation or imitation of the author

scenes.narration: Your first attempt fails. Should you try again, or change what you are trying?
scenes.visual: A paper glider falls; avatar inspects the fold.

scenes.narration: Napoleon Hill emphasized persistence. We can apply that idea while learning from feedback.
scenes.visual: Avatar keeps the destination but opens a notebook of observations.

scenes.narration: Psychological flexibility includes adjusting your response to the situation while acting on what matters.
scenes.visual: Show a route that bends around an obstacle.

scenes.narration: A student keeps the learning goal, but changes an ineffective study method.
scenes.visual: Passive rereading transitions to practice and checking mistakes.

scenes.narration: Repeating a harmful approach is not the only way to stay committed. Rest and support can belong in the plan.
scenes.visual: Avatar schedules a break and asks for guidance.

scenes.narration: What will you continue, what will you change, and when will you review the result?
scenes.visual: Three editable planning boxes animate in; reflection and source card.

episodes.narration_kind: Original educational adaptation; not a quotation or imitation of the author

scenes.narration: A rejection arrives, and your mind turns one event into a verdict about you.
scenes.visual: A rejection letter casts a shadow labeled failure over the avatar.

scenes.narration: Hill used the image of a seed of benefit within adversity. We will treat that as a possibility.
scenes.visual: A small seed sits beside the letter; it does not automatically grow.

scenes.narration: Cognitive reappraisal means changing how you interpret a situation to change its emotional meaning.
scenes.visual: The event stays fixed while two interpretation cards appear.

scenes.narration: This rejection might contain feedback about fit, preparation, or what to try next.
scenes.visual: Avatar reads feedback and sorts useful information from unfair criticism.

scenes.narration: You do not have to find a benefit in every loss. Pain deserves room, too.
scenes.visual: Avatar pauses with a supportive friend; the seed remains optional.

scenes.narration: What does this event tell you, and what does it fail to prove about your worth?
scenes.visual: Shadow lifts enough to show the avatar; hold reflection and source card.

scenes.narration: You keep circling the same problem alone. Every idea seems to lead back to the start.
scenes.visual: Avatar walks a loop of tangled paths.

scenes.narration: Napoleon Hill’s mastermind principle emphasizes working with others toward a shared aim.
scenes.visual: Two original collaborators join; the loop opens into a planning table.

scenes.narration: Social support includes practical help, useful information, and emotional encouragement from other people.
scenes.visual: Show three distinct forms of support without magical imagery.

scenes.narration: A trusted peer spots a missing step. A mentor helps you test the next option.
scenes.visual: Peers compare plans; avatar retains the final decision.

scenes.narration: Agreement is not always good advice. Useful support can include a respectful challenge.
scenes.visual: One collaborator flags a weak assumption; group checks the evidence.

scenes.narration: Who could help you see this problem more clearly, and what specific help could you ask for?
scenes.visual: Avatar sends a specific request; reflection and readable source credits.
